title: R Packages
text:
I started developing R packages during the winter last year, primarily as a means to start compiling the mess of code I have been building for almost a decade. So far, I’ve been working primarily to build internal package for my employer, The Upstate Freshwater Institute.

ImportUtils
Terrible name, but works for us. Eventually I hope I can publish this one I think it could be useful to others. We switched from using YSI water quality sondes to In-Situ’s line of AquaTroll sondes with the 6600 line from YSI being phased out. A major difference from the YSI sondes is that the AquaTroll’s record the raw data.

title: Past Projects
text:
EPA Nine-Element Plans
I have worked to support a number of watershed nine-element plans during my tenure at UFI. My role has included the estimation of material (nutrient and sediment) loading coming from the land using empirical tools such as FLUX32 software and the R Package loadflex, the estimation of dreissenid mussel populations, and watershed modelling with GWLF-E (Generalized Watershed Loading Functions - Enhanced).

Owasco Lake (2019 - 2022)

Developed material loading estimates using FLUX32 software.
Watershed land use/land cover assessment using QGIS.
Estimated dreissenid mussel biomass, including both zebra and quagga mussels as a single profile with depth using linear regression models.



Skaneateles Lake (2021 - 2024)

Developed material loading estimates using FLUX32 software.
Watershed land use/land cover assessment using QGIS.
Estimated quagga mussel biomass as a series of depth profiles for each lake model segment using Bayesian heirarchical modelling.



Oneida Lake (complete - not released)

Developed material loading estimates using FLUX32 software.
Estimated dreissenid mussel biomass using sediment specific depth profiles within a linear modelling framework.



Sandy Creek (complete - not released)

Calibration and confirmation of GWLF-E watershed models for each of 13 HUC-12 watersheds under study.
Primary author of modeling report, including sensitivity analysis, model calibration, and management scenario runs reporting.



Otsego Lake (in-progress)

Data GAP analysis to identify critical data needs for completing the nine-element process.
Quality Assurance Project Plan (QAPP) development for water quality sampling and dreissenid mussel collection components.
Developed material loading estimates using the USGS loadflex R package.




Lake Management Plans
Plymouth Reservoir (SUNY Oneonta BFS Technical Report #32)

During my first year of the MS program, our cohort collaboratively developed an interim management plan for a small reservoir in central New York.
Highlights included the creation of a bathymetric map, fisheries survey, and water quality analysis, resulting in recommendations for management actions to protect recreational use of the waterbody.

Butterfield Lake (SUNY Oneonta BFS Occasional Paper #66)

My thesis included study of coliform bacteria, fisheries, macrophytes, zooplankton, dreissenid mussels, water quality, and nutrient loading.
The culmination was a list of recommended actions to protect water quality and best uses of Butterfield Lake.

Ballston Lake

UFI and EcoLogic LLC collaborated to complete field sampling of this unique lake in Eastern NY. It is a meromictic lake, meaning that a portion of the water column never mixes to the surface.




Myself holding a sample from the deep “monimolimnion” layer of Ballston Lake.



My roles included field sampling, GIS analysis of the watershed, nutrient loading analysis using available historical data and GWLF-E watershed modeling, and review of report text.

Hyde Lake

Polymictic lake in Northen NY with a unique bathymetry.
My roles included field sampling, GIS analysis of the watershed, compilation and analysis of historical water quality data, and writing and review of the final report.

Hatch Lake & Bradley Brook Reservoir

I was the primary investigator who reviewed three decades of historical data on two man-made reservoirs in central NY.
Using a combination of time series analysis, watershed modeling, GIS analysis, and site visits I was able to provide context to the lake association on recent changes to their waterbodies.



River Herring Growth
Utilizing data from the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries Age and Growth lab, I evaluated growth patterns among six spawning runs in coastal Massachusetts. This work included the use of back-calculation of length at age using the RFishBC package, then fitting those data to von-Bertalanffy growth models. This was the project where I was formally introduced to the use of Bayesian heirarchical modeling with JAGS via the R2jags package.

title: NRT
text:
Near Real Time Environmental Monitoring
The Upstate Freshwater Institute has always had a toe in the world of environmental monitoring including weather and water quality conditions. We often take things one step further by linking monitoring equipment to cellular modems so that the data can be viewed in near real time. Some of these systems produce data that are public facing, and I have become intimately involved with the construction, maintenance, and deployment of them. In fact, it’s probably become my primary role when I am out in the field. The work can be particularly challenging due to the harsh nature of mixing electronics with water in unpredictable lake environments.

Lake Ontario
UFI maintains three monitoring buoys on Lake Ontario, consisting of meteorological (wind, temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation), water quality (temperature, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, pH, chlorophyll), and wave (height, direction, period) and current sensors. In addition, each has webcams attached, including one that has an underwater camera (Sodus Point).



One of UFI’s Lake Ontario monitoring buoys.


These stations are monitored almost continuously throughout the year, with the large summer buoys being replaced by a “winter stick” setup for overwinter deployments. The winter season does not include meteorological data, and the surface system consists of a homemade PVC pipe containing the cellular model and antenna. We are continuously evolving the stick system to be rugged against the brutal conditions on Lake Ontario.
Data from the buoys are used by academic, federal, and state researchers for a number of projects related to the health of Lake Ontario. Additionally, the recreating public has increasingly become aware of the data and use it to help make safe decisions on when conditions on the lake are favorable. Currently, funding is provided through Great Lakes Observing System (GLOS), however, we are always seeking alternative funding sources to keep the buoys “afloat”. The underwater camera is currently funded by a grant through the NOAA National Marine Sanctuary Fund. Unfortunately, this fund will be dissolved at the end of 2026. We would like to keep the underwater camera running next season if we can fund it, since we now have the equipment and all the valuable wisdom from the first year of trying to keep the cameras working.


Otisco Lake
UFI currently hosts a profiling buoy on Otisco Lake, outfitted with a meteorological station and a water quality sonde that collects water quality profiles twice daily. The goal of this effortis to collect data in support of future water quality funding for the lake. My role with the buoy is primarily rigging, deployment, and maintenance. The buoy is funded by the Otisco Lake Preservation Association.


Onondaga Lake
The flagship UFI monitoring station, the Onondaga Lake buoy, sporting a meteorological station and water quality profiler, has been in place over 30 years. Similar to Otisco, my role is primarly related to physical deployment, retrieval and maintenance tasks.


Other
Skaneateles Lake -

Monitoring of turbidity to evaluate levels near municipal water intakes
Collaboration with SUNY ESF to log water temperature data at various depths

Tributary Monitoring
Maintenance of NRT equipment monitoring water quality variables in a number of streams across NYS. Many of these projects support the nine-element process.

title: David Andrews
text:
Senior Research Scientist
Upstate Freshwater Institute, Syracuse NY
I am just a guy who tried to follow his passion for the outdoors, always wanting to be out on the water but often found stuck behind a growing block of computer screens. I have a passion for marine systems, particularly the Gulf of Maine, despite my currently landlocked position in decidedly less salty waters.
I currently support a number of projects related to freshwater science and management throughout New York State both through deployment and maintenance of near real time monitoring systems, as well as data analysis and reporting. I am always working towards efficient tools enabling reproducible research to help our environmental managers do their jobs more effectively.


Education
PhD in Environmental Biology, State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry | In progress
MS in Lake Management, State University of New York at Oneonta | 2019
BS in Aquatics and Fisheries Science, State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Foresty | 2012

title: My Story
text:
I should title this page “Well that explains a lot!”

Early Life
I had a decidedly unique upbringing. I was raised in the central Adirondack Park of New York State, in the state’s smallest county by population (Hamilton). I graduated from Long Lake Central as the valedictorian in a grade of 7 students. My best friend was the saludatorian, and at one point it was just the two of us in middle school. We started with 7 and ended with 7, and got close but never hit double digits (9 was our max). I actually wasn’t even supposed to attend Long Lake, my house was technically in the Tupper Lake school district. It was also located in the Town of Colton in St. Lawrence County, while our address was a Long Lake adresss (because of where the mailbox was, 5 miles from the house), while our phone number was a Tupper Lake number. If that’s confusing to you, I don’t blame you, if you found it interesting you’re not alone. It was interesting enough that an AP sports writer with ties to the region, Tim Reynolds, wrote an article during my senior year which made it all the way to the NY times. The article chronicled what I found normal; hours on the bus every day, parents who would sit in the parking lot at school to pick me up from away games based on his best guess of when we would return (no cell service in the park at that point), and a community of people so tight knit that they would fill the gymnasium every spring to watch 6 or 7 seniors walk across the stage.
But back to that bit about living in a black hole. My father was the camp ranger (caretaker) for the Boy Scouts of America for 35 years. As such we lived at Sabattis Scout Reservation, a 1,500 acre Boy Scout Camp located between Long Lake and Tupper Lake, 18 miles off of route 30, with 12 miles of dirt road (to get to the bus stop), and 5 miles of private road behind a locked gate. The camp was completely off-grid, with diesel generators for power, and solar panels at the house I grew up in. My family was there year round, with volunteers, staff and campers present only from June - August. We had no internet, satellite internet (we could get 3 channels via an aerial antenna on the roof), and only a land-line phone. Unfortunately, you may have heard, the camp recently sold to Open Space Institute and will eventually transfer to state ownership. I am grateful I will be able to go back when it becomes public land, but we lost a true gem where youth were able to grow and have real valuable learning outside of a classroom. At the risk of becoming overly sentimental, I will just say that growing up there, almost an hour from my school friends, I was implicitly aware of my unique situation. I spent most of my time outdoors, fishing, biking, hiking, hunting, and trapping. My mom started taking me along at her job as Assistant Forest Ranger on Low’s Lake when I was maybe 5 or 6. I would sit in the middle of the canoe and fish all day while she made her rounds, talking to people campling out, helping them to find an open campsite, reminding them of rules and regulations, fire safety, things of that nature. I would have fished sunup to sundown if she let me.
When I was maybe 11 or 12 I started hanging out down in the Boy Scout Camp, primarily at the “trip center” where I would sail around in sunfish sailboats, tend a campfire, and generally pester the director there, who would oblige me when he could with a game of “balance wars”, where two people would stand at opposite ends of a windsurfer board, unable to touch each other, trying to make the other fall in the water. I spent a number of summers being a general nuisance to the staff, and disappearing into the woods with some of the other sons of staffers who weren’t old enough to work yet.
At the end of each summer, my family would vacation on the coast of Maine. I loved boogie boarding in the waves, fishing for striped bass, finding seashells and seaglass, and eating lobster. My love for the ocean came from those trips, despite the 55 degree water temps. It’s also where I got the worst case of hypothermia I’ve ever experienced after spending almost two hours snorkeling around in the rocks at low tide. Throughout high school it was much of the same. I eventually worked as staff at the scout camp, starting out teaching first year scouts, then working commissary, scoutcraft (think knots, orienteering, and wilderness survival), and eventually becoming a lifeguard, working the waterfront, I was mountain bike director the summer prior to college, and finally being my dads assistant for a summer. I know I missed out on a lot in town during those summers, but I also got to experience a lot and meet a ton of people, some of whom I am still close with today.


College v1 - Undergrad
Upon graduation, I enrolled at SUNY ESF in Syracuse, thanks in large part to my mother, who forced me to fill out the forms, and dragged me to friends houses in town who had internet access so we could fill out financial aid forms and the like. I actually never wanted to go to college, but also didn’t have a real conviction towards any particular career path. So off to Syracuse, starting undeclared at ESF in the fall of 2008, which was a rare thing at a school with pretty specialized majors. They told me I had to decide by the end of the fall term or I probably wouldn’t be able to graduate on time. Since I was undeclared I got to choose a freshman seminar to attend instead of the program specific one that majors take, and I chose the Environmental Science seminar since they had a different professor come in to talk each week. I think it was the third week when a professor came and talked about fisheries and it just clicked, this is what I want to do.
Despite my lackadaisical approach to college at first, I am grateful to have traveled that path. I met my wife thanks to the school sticking me in a single dorm room (don’t worry there were two of us, thankfully we got along) at the end of the girls hall for some reason. Thanks to her there is a catalog of photographs of my time at ESF, otherwise I doubt I’d have much to remember it by. And despite my original plan of attending a school where I could play soccer (I was passionate about it in high school, but looking back I wasn’t ever that good at it, I could just run a lot), I found myself at the woodsmen practice field one night, having hitched a ride with a couple of guys who showed up in my dorm and were heading there, who I honestly never saw again. Being on the woodsmen team became a large part of my identity at school; it was one of the greatest experiences of my time there. Generally a great group of people, and in hindsight we learned a lot by organizing and running the team, which was a club for the first two years and became wrapped under the athletic program at the start of my junior year. We traveled to Maine, Canada, and of course all over NY to compete, with the year culminating in the conclave wide “spring meet”. The culmination worked out perfect; we never won a meet until our home meet our senior year. We had been working and building towards it, and then we ended up sweeping the big spring meet conclave event at Dartmouth, NH, the same place I attended my first spring meet freshman year. In addition, Stihl at that point sponsored a collegiate challenge, and I represented ESF to a second place finish at nationals. If I’d have won I would have earned an automatic bid into the rookie world championships. I often wonder if I’d have won there if I’d have continued with timbersports longer. As it were, that was the last time I picked up an axe competitively.
On the academic side I did well, spent too much time worrying about grades, took every field course that was water centric they offered, along with the few marine science related courses. I was stuck on a couple student committee’s and won a Chancellor’s award for my research efforts that I had won a fellowship for to work at the Cranberry Lake Biological Station for a summer. Ironically, that station was by distance the closest I ever attended school to my house, it just took an 8 mile bushwack through the woods to get there! One of my favorite experiences was the Tropical Ecology field experience my junior year spring break. We went to the island of Dominica, and I teamed up with a classmate who similarly felt that if we were going to be on a tropical island we should probably be swimming. So we got to spend our research days snorkeling the coral reefs surrounding the island. For the last two years at ESF I worked the Carrier Dome (now JMA Dome), changing the floor out between basketball and lacrosse games. I also spent a night on top with warm water hoses spraying off snow in the middle of a blizzard. That was pretty miserable work, but it did afford me the chance to have our commencement photo taken on the roof of the dome.

Home Again
I had done an equally terrible job making a plan for my progression into the working world as I had for my undergraduate program. I was also slightly delusional thinking that my biology degree meant I could get a full time job as a biologist. So I spent a fair amount of time applying to jobs I had no hope of landing, while splitting my time between home in the Adirondacks and my future wife’s parents place on Oneida Lake. A friends dad who owned his own contracting business in Long Lake offered me a job as a laborer while I applied for jobs. It’s funny how things work out, that job would a primary factor in my landing my technician role with the MA DMF later on because the biologist was looking for someone to do some light construction/fabrication prior to field season ramping up. In any case, I had kept the idea of becoming a fisheries observer in my back pocket because I was pretty sure I could get the job, but wasn’t sure I wanted it. In the end, I had to make a move and landed a gig as at “At Sea Monitor” out of Gloucester, MA beginning in April of 2013, nearly a year after I graduated. The move to Massachusetts sticks in my memory very vividly for a few reasons, the first being that I moved with no housing set up, and just what I could fit in my pickup truck for belongings. Second, unfortunately the day I left was the day of the funeral for one of “the boys” from Long Lake. Thom Ross died in a car crash, a short while prior, and I regret that I couldn’t stick around for the service. It was the third time we lost a member from our small group of friends; my classmate Karl “Wil” Geiger drowned near the end of summer heading into 8th grade at just 12 years old, and then Caleb Austin to another car crash in 2011. These losses seemed extra poignant given the size of our town, and perhaps they played a part in solidifying the relationships among our friend group that have lasted to this day. In any case, the move was an exciting, but emotional one.


“Salt Life”
I could write a book on my experiences in Gloucester; we fit a lot of living into a few years. I spent two years going to sea as an At Sea Monitor, all the way to the International border with Canada (the Hague Line), for up to 13 days. I learned a lot about the fishing industry, and life at sea, got to sea some incredible sights from whales and dolphins, tuna, sharks, and all manner of sea life, to storms and waves. I ate some interesting food, mostly good, some surprising (microwaved lobster anyone?), and some I’d prefer to skip if it were offered again (anything liver, boiled fish). I honestly never felt nervous about those trips at the time, but looking back my lack of nerves may have been misplaced. One year after I was on one boat, it sank off the coast of Maine. Luckily, the whole crew survived the ordeal after spending hours in a life raft. Perhaps the moist poignant reminder was this past year, with the loss of the FV Lily Jean out of Gloucester, including the observer, who worked my job, for my company, out of my home port. May they rest in peace in calm winds and following seas.
That was a lot of doom and gloom all at once, but I do think it’s important to recognize those events, as they remind us of the fragility of life and to try and soak it up when we can. My time in Gloucester was filled with plenty of soaking. While the observer job was unconventional, it afforded me lot’s of full days off to recreate on the coast. Fishing for striped bass, with squid I caught the night before, from the beach at 1AM was pure bliss. I also found out in Massachusetts you could dive recreationally for lobster. I would typically be able to find at least enough for a meal just along the coast. I also would carry a knife, since it was illegal to have a speargun while lobstering, and had about a 50% success rate knifing winter flounder when I came across them.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text: Me and my daughter ice fishing Oneida Lake.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
Why Oneida Lake?
I have an intimate connection with Oneida Lake. My in-laws live on the North Shore, and ever since college I’ve been visiting the lake to fish, swim, and boat. Now that I live a short drive away, I spend a great deal of my weekends on Oneida.
Like many other people who use the lake, I’ve also followed along with the Oneida Lake Diehards and Oneida Lake Anglers Facebook groups.
One theme that comes up repeatedly is a simple question:
“What are the conditions on the lake right now?”
People want to know about wind, waves, and water temperature before making the trip. Shore-based webcams have helped fill that gap over the years, but several have come and gone.
Given my background and my company’s experience with on-lake monitoring and near-real-time data systems, I started wondering whether the Oneida Lake community could collectively support something more permanent: a dedicated monitoring buoy that makes lake conditions publicly available.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
This isn’t starting from scratch
The Upstate Freshwater Institute (UFI) already operates several near-real-time monitoring buoys that provide publicly available information for people recreating on local waterbodies. Our flagship station has been located on Onondaga Lake since 2000, with publicly available data hosted by UFI starting in 2012.
UFI is also currently monitoring four lakes in Allegany and Harriman State Parks, as well as water quality in a western New York stream for research and regulatory projects.
As a result, we already have much of the infrastructure and expertise needed to operate a monitoring buoy. UFI also has several buoys in storage that have been used for previous projects, including physical components and mooring equipment.
That significantly reduces the cost of getting a new monitoring buoy onto Oneida Lake.
The primary remaining costs are specialized monitoring equipment that is already committed to other projects for 2027, along with the personnel time required to outfit, deploy, maintain, and retrieve the buoy.

Existing Support
Upstate Freshwater Institute
My current employer is willing to contribute considerable equipment to offset startup costs including the actual buoy hull, mooring system, and critical hardware including the datalogger (“brains”) and cellular modem, equaling ~$6 - 8,000.
Cornell
I visited the field station in July 2026 and spoke with Jim Watkins, the acting director. He expressed his support for the idea, and we are currently in talks about use of the field station docks as a staging area for our operations.
If the project moves forward, Cornell may also be interested in using the buoy for research on Oneida Lake.
Oneida Lake Association
UFI has submitted a formal proposal to OLA for a collaboration to support a buoy and to establish efficient, transparent mechanisms for handling fundraising proceeds. Updates will be posted here as the proposal is reviewed.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
What would the buoy provide?



UFI engineer troubleshooting a Lake Ontario buoy, with MET station in background.


The initial goal is to provide the information that would be most useful to people using the lake.

1. Wind and weather
We use all-in-one meteorological stations from Young that measure:

Wind speed
Wind direction
Atmospheric pressure
Relative humidity
Air temperature

An internal compass allows the station to accurately determine wind direction. The initial cost estimate is based on purchase of only this station.


2. Water temperature
A thermistor chain would provide water temperature at multiple depths. For 2027, we would include a thermistor if funding is sufficient to purchase.
These can be custom ordered depending on how many sensors are needed. A base model with three sensors costs approximately $1,500, with additional sensors costing approximately $350 each.
Water temperature would be useful to anglers and other lake users, while also providing valuable information about the lake’s seasonal mixing and stratification to students and researchers.


3. Wave conditions
Wave height is considerably more expensive to monitor than wind or temperature.
One possibility would be to eventually purchase a Sofar Spotter Buoy, which is specifically designed to measure wave conditions.
Another possibility would be to develop a wave model that predicts conditions throughout the lake using wind speed, wind direction, and fetch. This could potentially provide wave predictions for the entire lake rather than measurements from a single point.
However, developing a reliable model for Oneida Lake would require significant engineering time, and the lake’s relatively shallow depth and numerous islands would make the modeling more complicated. For that reason, a dedicated wave sensor is probably a longer-term goal.


4. Webcam
A camera mounted to the buoy would provide another way for people to see lake conditions.
A GoPro and the necessary cables would cost approximately $750. These systems can be somewhat finicky, but they are relatively inexpensive compared with other monitoring equipment.
Because of data-transmission limitations, we typically record approximately 15 seconds of video at the top of every hour rather than maintaining a continuous live feed.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
What does it cost?
The initial challenge is that startup costs are considerably higher than the annual cost of keeping the platform operating.
For a basic monitoring buoy consisting primarily of a meteorological station, I estimate the initial cost at approximately:

$~17,000 to build the buoy
That includes a meteorological station equipment that would still need to be purchased, as well as the personnel time required to build and deploy the system.
Some critical equipment is already available through UFI, which helps reduce the total cost.

Datalogger — approximately $1,600 The datalogger is essentially the brain of the system, collecting and storing the sensor data.
Cellular modem + data transmission plan — approximately $350 Allows the buoy to transmit data back to shore.
Buoy hull and moorings — approximately $3 - 5,000. UFI Has a number of hulls in our inventory suitable to Oneida Lake.




Buoy hulls in storage at UFI.


Once deployed, I estimate the cost to operate the site at approximately:


$15,000 per season
That assumes two days to prep and deploy the buoy, one day to retrieve it at the end of the season, and three additional trips for maintenance or repairs. There is also time included to maintain the webpage interface, and time to clean, store and prep the buoy in the off season.
This estimate does not include major purchases of additional sensors directly, however, unused funds beyond what is required for routine maintenance and operation can be carried forward for equipment purchases.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
Where could this lead?
The meteorological station would be only the beginning.
Once a platform is established on the lake, additional sensors could be added as funding and equipment become available.
UFI already operates or has experience with several types of equipment that could eventually be incorporated into the platform.

Water Temperature
“Thermistor chains” can be custom configured to provide water temperature data at known depths

Public interest for recreation
Research interest to support lake management decisions
Moderate cost, depending on number of sensors ($1,500 for three sensors plus $350 per additional sensor)



Webcam

Provide on the water view of conditions for recreation
Outreach opportunity for community organizations
Affordable ($750 - $1,000)



Wave Data

Critical for safe recreation
Supplement to just wind speed and direction
More expensive to monitor ($5,000 + for just equipment, additional deployment and retrieval costs depending on equipment used)



Multiparameter water-quality sonde
These instruments can be configured to measure:

Water temperature
Conductivity
pH
Dissolved oxygen
Turbidity
Chlorophyll
Cyanobacteria

These are expensive instruments, and I wouldn’t expect them to be the first priority for a community-funded project. However, if a platform is already established on Oneida Lake, UFI and/or Cornell could potentially take advantage of it for research when equipment is available.


Underwater camera
UFI has been developing an underwater camera system on Lake Ontario this season. We’ve experienced some growing pains, but have had enough success to plan a redeployment next season incorporating what we’ve learned.
The major challenges are keeping biological growth from obscuring the camera and protecting the camera in an underwater housing. The system currently costs approximately $5,000–8,000.
An underwater camera on Oneida Lake could eventually provide a fascinating long-term record of conditions beneath the surface.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
Where would the buoy go?
I would aim to place the buoy in the deepest part of Oneida Lake, offshore of Cleveland, NY.
There are two major reasons for this location.
First, it is approximately mid-lake and in open water, making it a reasonable location for monitoring conditions representative of a large portion of the lake.
Second, the deepest part of the lake is particularly valuable from a scientific perspective. UFI is interested in better understanding the lake’s mixing regime, and a deep-water monitoring station would provide an opportunity to measure conditions that aren’t captured by shoreline observations.
In particular, temperature and dissolved oxygen measurements could help document seasonal stratification and oxygen depletion in the deepest water.
The location would also provide a useful combination of public information and scientific value: the same platform that tells someone how windy it is on the lake could also contribute to a long-term record of how Oneida Lake is changing.
While this would be the optimal location, it may be necessary to adjust due to the high volume of boat traffic on the lake. Final location will be decided on a basis of providing valuable information while ensuring public safety.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
text:
The goal for 2027
We don’t need to build the ultimate Oneida Lake monitoring station on day one.
If we can get a basic meteorological station onto the lake for the 2027 season, I would consider that a huge success. Depending on fundraising success, it may only be feasible to build a shore-based station in the first season, then expand onto the water in following years with additional funding support.
From there, the platform could become something much more valuable over time.
Additional funding could support:
Weather → Water temperature → Webcam → Waves → Water quality → Research
The more sensors we can support, the more useful the platform becomes to both the people who enjoy Oneida Lake and the scientists who study it.

title: Oneida Buoy Funding
section: Could the Oneida Lake community make this happen?
text:
Could the Oneida Lake community make this happen?
I think it is worth trying.
More than 32,000 people follow Oneida Lake Diehards, and more than 17,000 follow Oneida Lake Anglers. Obviously, not everyone in those groups lives on the lake, uses the lake regularly, or would be interested in supporting a project like this.
But we don’t need everyone.
If a few thousand people who fish, boat, swim, or otherwise enjoy Oneida Lake thought this was worthwhile, a few dollars per person could get the first platform on the water.
And unlike a one-time event or temporary project, the goal would be to create something that could provide useful information every ice-free season for years to come.
For anglers and boaters, that means having better information about conditions before heading out.
For scientists and resource managers, it means another long-term source of environmental data from one of New York’s most important recreational lakes.
And for everyone who loves Oneida Lake, it would be a community-funded piece of infrastructure that belongs to all of us.
That’s the idea. Now I’m trying to find out whether the community thinks it’s worth making happen.

title: Research
text:
Dressenid Mussels and Their Impacts on Skaneateles Lake, NY











(a) Quagga mussels on rocks.











(b) SCUBA diver collecting mussels.







Figure 1



My PhD research centers on two species of benthic bivalves which are invasive to North America; zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha) and quagga mussels (Dreissena bugensis). These mussels are capable of significant alteration of their environment and are known as “ecosystem engineers” for their capacity to alter invaded systems. As filter feeders, dreissenid mussels remove particulates from the water column, and either utilize them as food, or spit them back out, at which point living cells may survive or not. Through these processes, the typical effect of a mussel invasion is increased water clarity and elevated rates of nutrient cycling. However, there are many factors that result in the unique impacts that a waterbody undergoes resulting from invasion such as the size and structure of mussel population, the relative trophic state (how productive a waterbody is), and whether a waterbody is mixed regularly or thermally stratifies seasonally. To evaluate impacts in Skaneateles Lake, my research has three foci:

Methods for rapid assessment of mussel populations using underwater imagery
Assessment of the mussel population in Skaneateles Lake in 2021 and methods used for dreissenid population surveys
Water quality impacts of dreissenid mussels in Skaneateles Lake



Cazenovia Lake Macrophytes
I’ve never been much for botany, outside of a keen interest in dendrology and the son of two forestry majors, but since UFI took over the aquatic macrophyte survey on Cazenovia Lake from Bob Johnson at Cornell I have become quite familiar with at least the aquatic plant community of this one NYS lake! We have a paper out for review that explores the use of herbicides to control Eurasian watermilfoil (Myriophyllum spicatum) and how the plant community has responded across the 20+ years of survey data.


Sea Lamprey Migration Phenology
My time in New York has been punctuated by a shift away from fisheries work, but I have been trying for the past few years to launch a project exploring the use of environmental DNA (eDNA) to track the movement of sea lamprey from Lake Ontario tributaries as they make their journey to the lake as juveniles. This has been a historically difficult life period to study because they are hard to trap, requiring facing fyke nets upstream during the fall, during high flows. The use of eDNA could offer an opportunity to monitor these movements without the need for nets, but we need to first determine if the signal is powerful enough compared to its variability to definitively attribute changes in detection magnitude to lamprey movement.
